sources.quote: Ultimately from Old Japanese. Cognate with 面 (omote). Derived as a compound of 面 (omo, “face”) + 手 (te, “hand; direction, side”), basically meaning "face-wards; facing side".
The term omote in general is attested since the Nihon Shoki of 720. The 表 spelling for this word is attested from roughly 1000.
Cognate with Okinawan 表 (umuti).

quotes: From Middle Chinese 表 (MC pjiewX). Attested in a portion of the Shoku Nihongi dated to 703.

examples.ja: 下駄を突っかけて表に飛び出した。
examples.en: I slipped on my geta and dashed outside.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *yamu.

quotes: Doublet of 泊(と)める (tomeru).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ut-. Cognate with Miyako 打つぃ (utsï).

sources.quote: ⟨oto₂⟩ → */otə/ → /oto/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ətə.
Appears in the late 1400s with the geminate pronunciation /otto/. This reading is very rare, and appears to have fallen out of use.

quotes: */ʔiəm/ → /əmʉ/ → /omʉ/ → /oɴ/
From Middle Chinese 音 (MC 'im).
⟨to₂⟩ → */tə/ → /to/
Apheresis of 音(おと) (oto) above.

The drop is likely due to lexicalization of compound terms (such as with the possessive particle の (no)), which would necessitate contraction of /CV oto/ to /CVto/ (e.g. no oto → noto) due to Old Japanese rules against vowel hiatus. This contracted form could have then been reanalyzed as a distinct form of the word.
⟨ne₂⟩ → */nəɨ/ → /ne/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712, with the phonetic spelling 泥.

The original meaning appears to have been "a sound or cry, as made by an insect, bird, or beast", likely related to the verb for making such a sound, 鳴く (naku, “to make a sound; to cry out”), as well as its doublet 泣く (naku, “to cry, to weep”). It is also likely related to 鳴る (naru, “to sound; to ring”).
From Middle Chinese 音 (MC 'im).
The kan'on pronunciation, so likely a later borrowing.

meaning: to be empty (in reference to people), to be less crowded

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, first attested in the Kojiki (712 CE).
Various theories exist regarding the ultimate derivation:
* Possibly a shift from verb 明かす (akasu, “to pass”).
*: */akasu/ → */akusu/ → /asu/
* Possibly an apophonic form of or cognate with 朝 (asa, “morning”).
The kanji spelling is an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 明日.

quotes: Shift in meaning from 朝 (ashita, “next morning”), itself cognate with 朝 (asa, “morning”).
The kanji spelling is from Chinese 明日 (míngrì).
/mʲau nʲiti/ → /mʲɔːɲit͡ɕi/ → /mʲoːɲit͡ɕi/
From Middle Chinese compound 明日 (MC mjaeng nyit).
From a later borrowing of Chinese 明日 (míngrì), using the 漢音 (kan'on, literally “Han sound”).
Rare reading.

quotes: ⟨upe₂⟩ → /*upai̯/ → /upe/ → /ufe/ → /uwe/ → /ue/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *upay.
Unbound apophonic form of uwa, ancient upa (see below).
/upa/ → /ufa/ → /uwa/
From Old Japanese. The combining form of ue, ancient upe (see above).
⟨upe₂⟩ → ⟨pe₂⟩ → */pe/ → /fe/ → /he/ (→ /e/)
Short-form of or shift from ue, ancient upe (see above). Realized as -e in some compounds.
⟨kami₁⟩ → */kamʲi/ → /kami/
From Old Japanese. Already apparent in ancient texts such as the Kojiki (c. 712 CE) and the Man'yōshū (c. 759 CE).
Distinct from 神 (⟨kami₂⟩ → kami, “Shinto deity”).
/kami/ → /kamʉ/ → /kaɴ/
Contraction of Old Japanese ⟨kami₁⟩. Spelled in ancient works as かむ (kamu) prior to the development of the ん (n) kana.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 生 (MC sraeng|sraengH, “alive; fresh; raw; unprocessed”). The 漢音 (kan'on) reading, so likely a later borrowing from Middle Chinese.

quotes: From Old Japanese. Numerous derivatives already in use in the Heian period.
Likely a contraction from 生き (iki, “life, living; freshness”).
From Middle Chinese 生 (MC sraeng|sraengH). The 呉音 (goon) reading, so likely the initial borrowing from Middle Chinese.
Inherited from Old Japanese. There are various theories about the origin of this term, including:
* Apheresis of 生ふ (opu → pu → fu, “to grow”) used predicatively
* Contraction of 原 (paru → pu → fu, “field”)
* Contraction of 生ゆ (payu → pu → fu, “to grow”) used predicatively

examples.ja: 死は生の正反対である。
examples.en: Death is the antithesis of life.

meaning: to hold (v.t.) (written expression), to embrace, to harbor

sources.quote: /udaku/ → /idaku/
Shift from earlier udaku.

This reading is possibly cited to a work from roughly 850 CE. However, that citation is phonologically ambiguous, and may represent the reading udaku instead. The first unambiguous citation for the idaku reading is in the Tosa Nikki of roughly 935 CE.
While there are numerous examples of mu shifting to u in various words, the mu- → u- → i- shift is unusual, and is shared only by mubara → ubara → ibara (茨, “bramble, briar”).
Found more commonly in 和(わ)文(ぶん) (wabun, “texts written primarily in native Japanese vocabulary”).

quotes: /idaku/ → /daku/
Shift from idaku.

Compare the shift of 茨(いばら) (ibara, “bramble, briar”) → 薔薇(ばら) (bara, “rose”), or Classical いでる (ideru) and いだす (idasu) to modern 出(で)る (deru, “to come out, to appear”) and 出(だ)す (dasu, “to take out, to put out”).
First cited to the Utsubo Monogatari of roughly 999 CE.
⟨mudaku⟩ → /mudaku/ → /udaku/
Shift from Old Japanese 抱(むだ)く (mudaku), in turn possibly a compound of 身(む) (mu, “body”, combining reading) + 綰(た)く (taku, “to gather in the hands; to work or operate something with the hands”).
First cited to a text from roughly 810 CE.

This reading is encountered more in the context of 漢(かん)文(ぶん)訓(くん)読(どく) (kanbun kundoku, “the Japanese reading of texts written primarily in a variety of Classical Chinese”), and it fell out of use in roughly the Kamakura period.

The four kanji spellings of this term, 金 (“gold”), 銀 (“silver”), 銅 (“copper”), and 鉄 (“iron”), hint at the importance of each of these four metals in ancient Japan.

sources.quote: Alteration of kara, “qualities, characteristics”. Originally only found as a suffix. The kara changes to gara as an instance of rendaku (連濁). The rendaku pronunciation was then later used independently.

quotes: Change in meaning from 枝(え) (e, historically ye, “branch, stem”).

From Old Japanese. Used in the Kojiki. Generally regarded as cognate with 黴(かび) (kabi, “mold”), from the shared idea of sprouts or shoots. Appears to be the noun stem of Old Japanese verb かぶ (kabu) (source of modern 黴(かび)る (kabiru, “to go moldy”)), with probable original meaning of to sprout.
/kabi/ → /kapi/ → /kaɸi/ → /kawi/ → /kai/
Alteration of kabi.
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kara. Origin of particle から (kara, “from, because”).
In light of the stem sense, probably derived semantically from origin, source meanings.
Compare also Korean 가락 (garak), similarly used as a counter for long and slender objects.
Cognate with 束(つか) (tsuka, ancient unit of length, equivalent to the amount covered from pinky to forefinger when gripping something; analogous to English hand).

Both likely derive from verb 付(つ)く (tsuku, “to set to, to attach, to accompany”), particularly as seen in modern Japanese idioms such as 手(て)を付(つ)ける (te o tsukeru, “to set one's hand to something”), 手(て)が付(つ)く (te ga tsuku, “to start using something”, literally “one's hand sets on something”).
Nominalization of verb 付(つ)く (tsuku, “to attach”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 管 (kuda, “pipe, tube”).
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 and the Man'yōgana of 759 with the ideogrammatic spelling of 小角 (literally “small horn”).

quotes: /kwan/ → /kan/
From Middle Chinese 管 (kuɑn^X, “pipe, tube”).
The pipe sense is traced back to the writings of Zhuangzi, already an influential text in Japan in the 700s.

The brush handle sense is traced back to the text of the 詩経 (Shikyō, “Classic of Poetry”), an Old Chinese poetry anthology written from the 11th to 7th centuries BCE and already influencing Japanese writing since the mid-700s.
The wind instrument sense is sourced from the 延喜式 (Engishiki) of 927.

/siripe/ → /çirife/ → /çirie/
From Old Japanese. Found in the Nihon Shoki of 720, and phonetically as 志利弊 (siripe₁) in the Man'yōshū of 759.
Compound of 尻 (shiri, “butt, tail, rear”) + 方 (e, “side, facing, way, direction”).
From Old Japanese. Ultimate derivation unknown.

From Middle Chinese 後 (huwX, “after”). Classified as the kan'on, so likely a later borrowing. Compare modern Mandarin reading hòu.

sources.quote: From 明後 (myōgo-, “the ... after next ...”) + 日 (nichi, “day”).

quotes: /asate/ → /asat̚te/
Shift from earlier asate (see Etymology 2 below).
The kanji spelling is from myōgonichi (see Etymology 3 below).
/asu sarite/ → /asːarʉte/ → /asate/

Apparently recorded in the 名語記 (Myōgoki) etymology dictionary of 1263 as a shift from asusate, in turn from 明日去りて (asu sarite), itself a compound of 明日 (asu, “tomorrow”) + 去りて (sarite, modern 去って (satte), the conjunctive form of 去る (saru), “to pass”).
The kanji spelling is from myōgonichi (see Etymology 3).
